practice.title: Conscientiousness with Structured Meditation
agreedSteps: Utilize conscientiousness alongside your lamrim object for the day to tackle your delusion of choice -- let conscientiousness reframe another way to go deeper into your project.
Try gazing at the Buddha as a sitting meditation -- from simply looking with minimal control, to elaborating on Buddha's qualities, feeling his love, or developing gratitude.

Apply structured meditation in all practice: analytical meditation to find the object, placement meditation to hold it, then when distracted, stop completely, take about ten breaths to let the distraction energy subside, and return fresh.
steps: Consider dividing each meditation into rounds of analytical-then-placement shots -- even brief rounds create the habit of mental organization, which pays out in the long run.

When not in formal meditation, apply the same principle throughout the day: when distracted from any activity, pause and recognize the mind has wandered before returning, rather than whipping attention back.
practice.quote: Generally speaking, 10 minutes of a structured meditation is way more useful than 30 minutes of an unstructured meditation. Because the habit that's creating is one of organization, mental organization, mental discipline.

commentary.title: Analytical and Placement Meditation
content: How do we actually put Dharma teachings into practice? Through analytical and placement meditation. First, we take a critical look at each subject, trying to understand its meaning and relevance for our lives -- that's analytical meditation. Once we come to some conclusion about the object of meditation, we place our mind upon it single-pointedly -- that's placement meditation.

If we think that meditation means sitting with an empty mind, we will receive no benefit, no matter how long we meditate. Everything in Shantideva's text is an object for meditation. It is a big mistake to try to meditate on nothing. Without a proper object of meditation, there will be little to show from even a thousand years of sitting.

The whole process is like setting out on a journey. If we want to go to London but don't know which road to take, we might arrive in Manchester. Similarly, if we try placement meditation without first gaining a thorough understanding of the object through analytical meditation, our efforts will be wasted and many faults will arise.
commentary.quote: If we think that meditation means sitting with an empty mind, we will receive no benefit, no matter how long we meditate.

commentary.title: Structured Meditation
content: In Clear Light of Bliss, Geshe-la suggests dividing every meditation into eighteen subsections -- eighteen rounds of analytical and placement meditation shots, then done. Try to find the object through analysis, get some gist of it, get distracted -- that's subsection one. Try again, distracted within one second -- subsection two. Like that, until eighteen, then take a break.

Our mind is pattern-based -- it follows patterns. If we meditate in a sloppy way, that reinforces the habit to meditate sloppily next time. Trying is way better than not trying, but once we start trying, it's worth asking: do I have some bad habits on the cushion that I keep feeding? Can I tighten up the ship a bit?

The discipline is: analytical meditation, placement meditation, distracted -- stop with a disciplined mind. Pause, let all the distraction energy subside. About ten rounds of breathing meditation can help. Once it subsides, back in: analytical meditation, placement meditation. Not whipping the mind back into the meditation, which creates a fuzzy, ambiguous mess. We're creating an organized, structured meditation experience.

Ten minutes of structured meditation is way more useful than thirty minutes of unstructured meditation, because the habit being created is one of mental organization, mental discipline. A thirty-minute wandering meditation might reinforce discouragement, brainstorming, following whatever comes to mind -- stuff we then have to unlearn.
commentary.quote: Generally speaking, 10 minutes of a structured meditation is way more useful than 30 minutes of an unstructured meditation.

commentary.title: Meditating on a Buddha Image
content: In concentration sutra practice, Buddha encouraged training in concentration on a visualized Buddha image. There are several advantages. First, it's just an image -- way easier to concentrate on than a complex concept like bodhichitta, which has so many components. A child can visualize an image. Second, because Buddhas are outside samsara, meditating on a Buddha image automatically creates pure, uncontaminated karma -- an indestructible imprint that leads us out of samsara one day, regardless of motivation.

Third, it's easy to detect when our concentration has degraded. The image starts to fade -- that's mental sinking. We move on to other things -- mental excitement. It shakes a little -- subtle excitement. The grip fades slightly -- subtle sinking. With an abstract object like patience, how would we even notice?

It's also a completely safe and gentle meditation. The Buddhas love us knowing the entire mess in our mind and everything we've done and not done. They totally believe in us and are willing to go with us for the long haul, even thousands of lives to enlightenment. It's like having a friend we could go to after something awful happened -- someone who would just hold space, not want anything from us, not coach us out of any feeling. Buddhas are like that, but far greater.

On the days when we're so sick or tired we can't think, can't read a Dharma book, can't listen to a teaching -- just sitting and staring at Buddha is a perfect, complete practice. It's nice to know we've got that in our back pocket.
commentary.quote: The Buddhas love us knowing the mess in our mind and knowing everything that we've done and not done. And they totally believe in us. They're rooting us on.

commentary.title: What Is Conscientiousness
content: Conscientiousness is a mental factor that, in dependence upon effort, cherishes what is virtuous and guards the mind from delusion and non-virtue. It's like a general coordinating the whole show -- routing virtues forward, blocking delusions, directing mindfulness and alertness. It's really the mind that makes us actually value virtuous minds and want to oppose deluded ones.

Its opposite is recklessness -- a careless attitude leading to deluded activity through all three doors. Recklessness of body includes killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, intoxication. Recklessness of speech manifests as lying, divisive speech, hurtful speech, idle chatter. Recklessness of mind includes covetousness, malice, and wrong views.

Conscientiousness is different from sense of shame, which avoids non-virtue out of consideration for oneself, or consideration for others, which avoids non-virtue for others' sake. Those are two sides of one coin. Conscientiousness is bigger -- it's specifically about being really interested in growing our virtues and abandoning our delusions.

It's also different from moral discipline, which focuses more on the actions themselves. Conscientiousness is the why behind moral discipline -- the mind that values virtue and opposes delusion, so that we then engage in positive actions. As Geshe-la says, conscientiousness should be practiced in conjunction with mindfulness and alertness. Moral discipline is the application of conscientiousness.
commentary.quote: The definition of conscientiousness is a mental factor that, in dependence upon effort, cherishes what is virtuous and guards the mind from delusion and non-virtue.

commentary.title: The Lamrim Storehouse
content: As we go to more classes, retreats, and empowerments, we keep getting new ideas and practices. But there's a wrong way to do this called catastrophic forgetting -- lurching from one thing to the next. You're making a lovely stew, someone says potatoes are great, and you throw your stew out and scramble to make something new. Then someone mentions cake, and you throw the potatoes against the wall.

The correct approach is the lamrim storehouse analogy. Think of our practice as a storehouse or warehouse. Someone says potatoes are great -- cool, good to know, let me put that on the shelf. I know where it is and I'll grab it when I need it. I'm working on my stew here, and it's not going in the potato direction right now.

Our daily practice -- whether it's six-session guru yoga, a lamrim meditation, or some other heart practice -- that's the stew. New teachings go in the storehouse. The teacher's job is to share the Dharma; our job is to have the wisdom to integrate and store it where it belongs, without lurching from thing to thing.
commentary.quote: The teacher's job is to share the Dharma, and then we have to have the wisdom on how to use that and integrate that and store that where it's supposed to go. So we don't need to lurch from this to that.

commentary.title: Imperfect Trying
content: There's a distinction between our imperfect trying and the optimal way to practice. We're always doing our best, and it will be imperfect until we're a Buddha. But when a teacher explains the proper way to do something, we can't take that as an indictment on our imperfect attempt.

It's never a criticism, never a judgment. Our imperfect attempt is way better than not doing anything. But we also can't just stay at the imperfect trying state forever. We need to know the ideal and keep improving. These are two different things -- and both are true at the same time.

If teachers worry about this too much, they stop teaching people how to actually do things correctly, and then nobody grows. It's just 'yeah, good job, we're all doing our best here.' Comforting in the short run, but in the long run we don't break out of anything.

commentary.title: Floor Practice
content: All of Buddhist practice boils down to overcoming delusions and increasing virtues. Having a floor practice -- on our worst day, what do we do? -- is incredibly helpful. Something really simple and axiomatic: 'Today I'm going to do no harm,' which is another name for compassion. Or 'I'm just going to try to stay with love today.'

These aren't cop-outs -- they're beautiful, essential practices with everything in them. Having this decided in advance means that on those bad days, we feel completely good and encouraged: it's a floor day, and that's fine. Without a floor, we crash through level after level and can really go off the rails. With a sturdy, virtuous floor, we bounce back and are protected from going too far.
commentary.quote: On our worst day, what do we do? Having this formalized and decided is incredibly helpful.

commentary.title: The Momentum of Practice
content: Every action we perform reinforces a behavior. It's not just a one-off -- every action creates momentum to go toward that behavior even more. When we understand this, it makes us very mindful about what we say, think, and do, because we realize we're not just doing or not doing one thing -- we're reinforcing a pattern that will repeatedly happen.

This is related to the karmic principle of tendency similar to the cause, and also to the idea that karma increases -- there's not a linear relationship, but an expanding momentum. From the positive side, this is really encouraging. From the negative side, it gives us a helpful pause. Once we start to notice the pattern, at some point it clicks -- this is part of my life and how I want my life to be.
commentary.quote: Every action isn't just a one-off action. Every action reinforces a behavior and creates a momentum to go towards that behavior even more.

dataShares: Fran noticed the momentum of dedication practice -- doing it creates more doing it, and stopping creates more stopping. Returning to 'delighting in virtue' turned things around.
Marianne explored subtle impermanence by actively meeting situations halfway rather than staying stuck in fear, finding that just by engaging with life, everything shifts.
Anne intensified her concentration practice and found relief by asking the Buddhas for help rather than relying solely on her ordinary mind.
Suzanne practiced patient acceptance through a difficult week and wishing love while out, but struggled to maintain practice at home without structure.
Ryan noticed that wherever there was unhappiness, there was attachment -- and that dropping his lamrim practice was the root cause.
Mimi targeted attachment, arriving at a visceral recognition that attachment to desires is what keeps us cycling in samsara -- seeing it as an addiction and a hallucination.
